metadata.title: Chaco Canyon (Tsé Bił Ndzisgaii) — Georeferenced Archaeological Digital Twin
metadata.siteCode: 29SJ387 (Pueblo Bonito — Chaco Culture National Historical Park)

dataSources.name: Library of Congress — Historic American Buildings Survey (HABS No. NM-30 / LOC Control No. nm0107: Pueblo Bonito)
dataSources.details: 10-sheet measured architectural drawing set (1939–1941, delineated by Herbert K. Boone, CCC Indian Mobile Unit, NPS Branch of Plans and Design; LOC Call No. HABS NM,23-CHACA,1- / HABS NM,23-____,1-). Documents Master Key Plan (Title Sheet), Section No. 1 (Sheets 1–5: Rooms 174, 175, 176, 177, 225, and 226, including T-door on West Wall of Room 226, Corner Doorway in NE Corner of Room 225, and North Window of East Wall of Room 177), and Section No. 2 (Sheets 6–9: Rooms 178, 179, 235–242, and Kiva D with subfloor foot resonator and sealed doorways in Rooms 241–242). Public Domain (PD-USGov-HABS).

dataSources.name: National Park Service (NPS) — Chaco Center Archaeological Reports & Measured Site Plans
dataSources.details: Official NPS measured architectural plans and monographs by Stephen H. Lekson (Great Pueblo Architecture of Chaco Canyon, 1984, Reports of the Chaco Center No. 8), Thomas C. Windes, and W. James Judge (Public Domain, PD-USGov-NPS).

dataSources.name: OpenTopography — Chaco Canyon 0.5m Airborne LiDAR Survey (OT.042019.6342.1)
dataSources.details: 2016 airborne LiDAR survey (NM16_Dorshow) covering 135 km² of Chaco Culture National Historical Park at 12.15 pts/m², resolving Chacra Mesa sandstone cliffs, prehistoric road swales, and Great House mounds.

dataSources.name: OpenTopography — Bare-Earth DEM & Digital Surface Model (OTSDEM.042019.6342.1)
dataSources.details: High-resolution Digital Elevation Model (DEM) and Digital Surface Model (DSM) of the Chaco Wash floor, Fajada Butte (135m prominence), standing multi-story walls, and the 1941 Threatening Rock talus cone.

dataSources.name: U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) — 1877 W.H. Jackson Survey & 1920 AMNH / 1954 Smithsonian Monographs
dataSources.details: Public Domain 1877 USGS architectural plans and reconstructions (W.H. Jackson, 10th Annual Report), George H. Pepper (1920, AMNH Vol. 27), and Neil M. Judd (1954, 1964, Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections).

dataSources.name: NASA Science / Earth Observatory — Pueblo Bonito Cardinal & Solar Alignment (EO-5678)
dataSources.details: Documents that the half-moon (D-shaped) footprint of Pueblo Bonito is locked to the cardinal directions: the straight southern wall runs East–West and the perpendicular dividing wall points directly North to track seasonal sun cycles for planting and winter preparation.

features.phase: Stage I–II: Buried Sub-Court Foundation (AD 900–1040)

features.artifacts: Kiva-specific artifact inventory depends on excavation history (Judd 1921–1927; Pepper 1896–1899). Excavated roomblock kivas typically contain radial pilaster logs/sockets, central hearth ash, subfloor ventilator shafts, and dedicatory beads (Judd 1964).

features.name: Room 32
features.title: Room 32 — Ceremonial Staffs Antechamber
features.phase: Stage I: Old Bonito Crescent (AD 850–935)
features.masonry: Type I Tabular Sandstone Slabs & Mud Mortar
features.dendroDates: AD 862–919 (tree-ring dates on ceiling poles; Windes & Ford 1996)
features.artifacts: 375+ carved wooden ceremonial staffs (pahos) and crook sticks, a quiver of 81 reed arrows, turquoise-and-Spondylus shell mosaic cylinder baskets, feather-cloth robes, and 25+ Red Mesa Black-on-white vessels.
features.summary: Immediately south of Room 33 and providing the sole interior doorway (width ~0.52 m) into the Room 33 crypt, Room 32 (1.4 × 1.9 m, 2.7 m²) was excavated by George H. Pepper in 1896 (Pepper 1920). Pepper recorded 375+ carved wooden staffs (pahos) stacked in the northwest corner, a quiver of 81 reed arrows, and turquoise-and-shell mosaic cylinder baskets. Ceiling poles yielded tree-ring dates between AD 862 and 919 (Windes & Ford 1996).
features.excavator: George H. Pepper (Hyde Exploring Expedition, 1896; Pepper 1920, AMNH Vol. 27)
features.tinyEra: STAGE I OLD BONITO CORE • TREE-RING DATED AD 862–919

features.name: Room 228
features.title: Room 228 — Winter Solstice Corner Window
features.phase: Stage III–IV Southeast Wing (AD 1065–1115)
features.dendroDates: Late 11th to early 12th century (c. AD 1065–1110, Classic/Late Bonito phase)
features.artifacts: Exterior corner window aperture oriented ~120° ESE toward Winter Solstice sunrise (Reyman 1976), Chaco Black-on-white ceramic sherds, and hearth ash.
features.summary: Rooms 225 and 228 in the southeastern sector of Pueblo Bonito (Room 228 polygon: 4.4 × 5.8 m, 25.5 m²; Room 225 polygon: 3.5 × 5.9 m, 20.7 m²) feature exterior corner windows oriented toward azimuth ~120° East-Southeast. Field transit observations and photography by Jonathan E. Reyman (1976, Science 193(4257):1037–1038) confirmed that at Winter Solstice sunrise (December 21), a narrow beam of sunlight enters the corner windows of Rooms 225 and 228 and illuminates the opposite interior wall/corner.
features.excavator: Neil M. Judd (1923; Judd 1954, 1964) • Archaeoastronomy: Jonathan E. Reyman (1976, Science)
features.tinyEra: STAGE III–IV • APPROX. AD 1065–1110

features.artifacts: Kiva O remains largely unexcavated; most interior architectural details and any in-situ floor assemblage remain unknown. The bench, hearth, roof arrangement, roof height, and other interior features shown in this model are interpretive reconstructions based on comparable Pueblo Bonito kivas.
features.summary: Approx. 11.3 m exterior diameter. Because Kiva O remains largely unexcavated, its precise floor diameter and interior dimensions are uncertain. Classified as Type II masonry and constructed as a subterranean circular structure; its surviving exterior form can be documented, but most interior architectural details remain unknown. The bench, hearth, roof arrangement, roof height, and other interior features shown in this model are interpretive reconstructions based on comparable Pueblo Bonito kivas. Kiva O appears to predate Pueblo Bonito’s latest major architectural expansion; its exact construction date remains uncertain.

features.name: Great Kiva A
features.title: Great Kiva A — East Court Great Kiva
features.phase: Late 11th–Early 12th Century • Approx. AD 1075–1115
features.masonry: Type III Fine Banded Core-and-Veneer with 4 Square Rubble-Filled Masonry Columns & 34 Wall Niches
features.dendroDates: Late 11th–early 12th century construction (approx. AD 1075–1115); use and remodeling continued into the later 12th century
features.artifacts: Four large square rubble-filled masonry columns supporting the reconstructed timber roof, flanking a raised central firebox and paired subfloor masonry vaults; concentric masonry bench and 34 wall niches (found open and empty when excavated). Turquoise, shell, and mineral offerings are documented from dedicatory architectural and ceremonial contexts at Pueblo Bonito.
features.summary: Approx. 13.7 m interior floor diameter (~147.4 m²) and approximately 17.0 m exterior diameter (~227 m²; 16.0 m modern georeferenced footprint). Great Kiva A was built during Pueblo Bonito’s final major architectural expansion in the late 11th to early 12th century (approx. AD 1075–1115 construction), with use and remodeling continuing into the later 12th century. Integrated into the East Court architectural complex and surrounded by an encircling masonry bench, four massive square rubble-filled masonry columns supported the reconstructed timber roof (reconstructed ceiling height approx. 9 ft 7 in above the floor). The kiva also contained 34 wall niches, a formal northern entrance stairway, and paired masonry vaults flanking the raised central firebox (sometimes interpreted as foot drums, although their exact function remains uncertain). Turquoise and other colorful materials were deposited in ritual or dedicatory architectural contexts at Pueblo Bonito. Separately, a four-strand necklace containing approximately 2,500 turquoise beads was recovered elsewhere at Pueblo Bonito and should not be described as a Great Kiva A find.

features.name: Great Kiva Q
features.title: Great Kiva Q — West Court Great Kiva
features.phase: Classic Bonito Phase • Probably Mid-11th Century
features.masonry: Subterranean Coursed Sandstone with Encircling Bench & 4 Circular Masonry Roof-Post Settings
features.dendroDates: Probably mid-11th century (predates Great Kiva A; precise construction date uncertain)
features.artifacts: Four large wooden roof-support posts seated in circular masonry settings (visually and structurally distinct from the four square masonry columns of Great Kiva A), paired rectangular subfloor vaults, central firebox, encircling masonry bench, and a reconstructed southern entry stairway/antechamber.
features.summary: Approx. 12.1 m interior floor diameter (~115 m²) and approximately 14.6 m exterior diameter (12.6 m current georeferenced wall footprint). Great Kiva Q appears to predate Great Kiva A and probably belongs to an earlier major Pueblo Bonito construction phase, approximately around the mid-11th century; its precise construction date remains uncertain. Recessed into the West Court and surrounded by an encircling masonry bench, Great Kiva Q used four large wooden roof-support posts seated in circular masonry settings (which should not be interpreted as solid masonry columns like those of Great Kiva A), paired rectangular subfloor masonry vaults, and a central hearth or firebox. Archaeological reconstruction includes a southern stairway and antechamber, although aspects of this entrance reconstruction remain debated. The complete roof, wall height, and interior appearance shown here are interpretive reconstructions.
features.excavator: Neil M. Judd (National Geographic Society, 1924; Judd 1964) • NPS Measured Survey

features.tinyTitle: GREAT KIVA Q — WEST COURT GREAT KIVA
features.description: Appearing to predate Great Kiva A and probably belonging to an earlier mid-11th-century construction phase, Great Kiva Q is a recessed circular Great Kiva in the West Court with an encircling masonry bench, central firebox, paired rectangular subfloor vaults, and a reconstructed southern entry stairway/antechamber. Great Kiva Q used four large wooden roof-support posts seated in circular masonry settings—visually and structurally distinct from the four square masonry columns of Great Kiva A. The full roof timbering, upper wall height, and southern stairway appearance shown in the model are interpretive reconstructions.
keyPoints: Dating & Architecture: Great Kiva Q appears to predate Great Kiva A and probably belongs to an earlier major Pueblo Bonito construction phase, approximately around the mid-11th century (precise construction date remains uncertain). Recessed into the West Court and surrounded by an encircling masonry bench.

Roof Support & Floor Features: Four large wooden roof-support posts were seated in circular masonry settings. These should not be interpreted as solid masonry columns like those of Great Kiva A. Floor features include paired rectangular subfloor masonry vaults and a central hearth or firebox.

Entrance & Reconstruction: Archaeological reconstruction includes a reconstructed southern stairway and antechamber, although aspects of this entrance reconstruction remain debated. The complete roof, wall height, and interior appearance shown here are interpretive reconstructions.

features.name: Room 28
features.title: Room 28 — Cylinder Jar Cache & Cacao Residue
features.phase: Old Bonito Construction • Late 11th–Early 12th Century Cache Deposit
features.masonry: Multi-Phase Old Bonito & Remodeled Masonry (Wall Rebuilding, Subdivision & Reconstructed Upper Story)
features.dendroDates: Old Bonito construction; late 11th–early 12th century cache deposit
features.artifacts: Excavations recovered approximately 174 whole ceramic vessels from Room 28, including ~111–112 Chacoan cylinder jars (with roughly 99 concentrated together on a raised storage shelf/area), alongside ceramic bowls and pitchers, burned during a termination event around AD 1100. Chemical residue analysis tested five cylinder jar sherds from Pueblo Bonito and detected theobromine (Theobroma cacao) in three of them.
features.summary: The surviving Room 28 measures just under 8 m long and approximately 2.75 m wide at the surface. Earlier construction phases indicate that Room 28 and adjoining space were originally part of a substantially longer Old Bonito room before later partitioning and remodeling. Room 28 underwent several construction phases, including wall rebuilding, subdivision, and the addition of an upper story (reconstructed) during the 11th century. Excavators recovered approximately 174 whole ceramic vessels from Room 28, including 112 Chacoan cylinder jars. Around AD 1100, many of the vessels were deliberately arranged and burned during a termination event; roughly 99 cylinder jars were concentrated on a shelf or raised storage area, accompanied by turquoise and shell materials. Chemical analysis tested five pottery sherds from Pueblo Bonito; three produced theobromine, demonstrating the preparation or consumption of cacao beverages at Chaco, which reached the region through long-distance exchange networks originating in Mesoamerica.
features.excavator: George H. Pepper (Hyde Exploring Expedition, 1896; Pepper 1920) • Residue analysis: Patricia L. Crown & W. Jeffrey Hurst (2009, PNAS)
features.description: Originally part of the early Old Bonito northern arc and later remodeled and subdivided, with an added upper story. Excavators recovered approximately 174 whole ceramic vessels from Room 28, including ~111–112 Chacoan cylinder jars (with roughly 99 concentrated on a shelf or raised storage area) alongside bowls and pitchers, deliberately arranged and burned during a termination event around AD 1100. Chemical analysis tested five pottery sherds from Pueblo Bonito and detected theobromine—the biomarker for Theobroma cacao—in three of them.

features.tinyEra: OLD BONITO CONSTRUCTION • LATE 11TH–EARLY 12TH CENTURY CACHE DEPOSIT
features.tinyTitle: ROOM 28 — CYLINDER JAR CACHE & CACAO RESIDUE
keyPoints: Architecture: Earlier construction phases indicate that Room 28 and adjoining space were originally part of a substantially longer Old Bonito room before later partitioning and remodeling. Room 28 underwent several construction phases, including wall rebuilding, subdivision, and the addition of an upper story (interpretive reconstruction) during the 11th century.

Cylinder Jar Cache: Excavators recovered approximately 174 whole ceramic vessels from Room 28, including 112 Chacoan cylinder jars. Around AD 1100, many of the vessels were deliberately arranged and burned during a termination event. Roughly 99 cylinder jars were concentrated on a shelf or raised storage area, accompanied by turquoise and shell materials.

Cacao Evidence: Chemical analysis tested five pottery sherds from Pueblo Bonito. Three produced theobromine, demonstrating the preparation or consumption of cacao beverages at Chaco. Cacao could not have been grown locally and must have reached Chaco through long-distance exchange networks originating in Mesoamerica.

features.name: Room 249
features.title: Room 249 — Macaw Aviary & East Wing Chamber
features.phase: Stage III: East Wing Expansion (AD 1060–1085)
features.masonry: Type III Banded Core-and-Veneer with Ponderosa Lintels
features.dendroDates: Mid- to late 11th century construction (c. AD 1050–1085) • Direct AMS ¹⁴C on macaw remains (Watson et al. 2015, PNAS)
features.artifacts: 3 Scarlet Macaw (Ara macao) skeletons, a thick floor layer of compacted avian guano, adobe food/water bowls, and wooden perches set into the masonry walls (Judd 1954). Sequenced Chaco macaws fall within the same broader mitochondrial clade (Haplo6) with low diversity across closely related haplotypes.
features.summary: Excavated by Neil M. Judd (1921–1927; Judd 1954), Room 249 (2.1 × 2.7 m, 5.7 m²; reconstructed multi-story elevation is interpretive) in the East Wing yielded 3 Scarlet Macaw (Ara macao) skeletons, a thick floor layer of avian guano/droppings, adobe food and water bowls, and wooden perches set into the masonry walls. Pueblo Bonito has produced approximately 35 macaws plus 2 thick-billed parrots in recent reassessments of the collections. Ancient-DNA research on archaeological Scarlet Macaws from Chaco and the Mimbres region found extremely low mitochondrial diversity, consistent with a captive breeding population descended from a small founder group of unknown exact location, reaching Chaco through long-distance exchange networks. Nearby in the southeastern East Wing (Section No. 1, Rooms 174–177 and 225–226), Library of Congress HABS No. NM-30 (LOC Control No. nm0107, Sheet 5) documents the measured T-shaped doorway on the West Wall of Room 226 and the Corner Doorway in the NE Corner of Room 225.
features.excavator: Neil M. Judd (National Geographic Society, 1921–1927; Judd 1954) • AMS ¹⁴C: Watson et al. (2015) • aDNA: George et al. (2018)
features.description: East Wing aviary room (2.1 × 2.7 m, 5.7 m²) excavated by Neil M. Judd (1954), containing 3 Scarlet Macaw (Ara macao) skeletons, wooden wall perches, adobe bowls, and a compacted guano floor layer (Watson et al. 2015; George et al. 2018).

features.name: Room 38
features.title: Room 38 — Macaw-Keeping Room & Ritual Deposit
features.phase: Old Bonito Core • Macaw Use ca. AD 900–1040
features.masonry: Type I Tabular Sandstone with Adobe Plaster (Reconstructed Upper Story Is Interpretive)
features.dendroDates: Old Bonito core; macaw acquisition mostly AD 900–1040 (Watson et al. 2015)
features.artifacts: 14 scarlet macaw skeletons—12 associated with and embedded in a thick deposit of compacted bird guano (indicating live birds were kept in the room) and 2 intentionally placed in subfloor hollows—along with a turquoise-inlaid black jet frog. Sequenced Chaco macaws fall within the same broader mitochondrial clade (Haplo6) with low diversity across closely related haplotypes (George et al. 2018).
features.summary: Irregular room with maximum dimensions of approximately 9.2 × 5.4 m (40.7 m² polygon area); the reconstructed upper story is interpretive. Room 38 contained the remains of 14 Scarlet Macaws: twelve were associated with a thick deposit of bird guano, providing strong evidence that living macaws were kept in the room, and two additional macaws had been intentionally placed in floor hollows. The room also produced a carved jet frog ornament with turquoise inlay. Eleven macaws from Room 38 were included in direct AMS radiocarbon dating, demonstrating that macaws were present at Pueblo Bonito well before the traditional peak of Chacoan political and architectural development. Ancient-DNA research on archaeological Scarlet Macaws from Chaco and the Mimbres region found extremely low mitochondrial diversity, consistent with a captive breeding population descended from a small founder group whose precise location remains unknown; the birds ultimately derived from populations far south of Chaco and reached the region through long-distance exchange networks. Pueblo Bonito has produced approximately 35 macaws plus 2 thick-billed parrots in recent reassessments of the collections.
features.excavator: George H. Pepper (Hyde Exploring Expedition, 1897; Pepper 1920) • AMS ¹⁴C: Watson et al. (2015, PNAS) • aDNA: George et al. (2018, PNAS)
features.footprint_label: Irregular room with maximum dimensions of approximately 9.2 × 5.4 m (40.7 m² polygon area)
features.description: Early Old Bonito room within the northern roomblock (reconstructed vents, doors, perches, and upper-story details shown in the 3D model are interpretive). Excavations recovered 14 scarlet macaw skeletons—12 associated with and embedded in a thick deposit of bird guano, providing strong evidence that living macaws were kept in the room, and 2 intentionally placed in floor hollows—along with a turquoise-inlaid black jet frog. Radiocarbon and ancient-DNA studies show that macaw acquisition at Pueblo Bonito occurred mostly between AD 900 and 1040, and sequenced Chaco macaws fall within the same broader mitochondrial clade (Haplo6) with low diversity across closely related haplotypes, consistent with a restricted founder/breeding population.
features.tinyEra: OLD BONITO CORE • MACAW USE CA. AD 900–1040
keyPoints: Excavation: Room 38 contained the remains of 14 Scarlet Macaws. Twelve were associated with a thick deposit of bird guano, providing strong evidence that living macaws were kept in the room. Two additional macaws had been intentionally placed in floor hollows. The room also produced a carved jet frog ornament with turquoise inlay.

Radiocarbon Dating: Eleven macaws from Room 38 were included in direct AMS radiocarbon dating. The results demonstrate that macaws were present at Pueblo Bonito well before the traditional peak of Chacoan political and architectural development.

Origin & Genetics: Ancient-DNA research on archaeological Scarlet Macaws from Chaco and the Mimbres region found extremely low mitochondrial diversity, consistent with a captive breeding population descended from a small founder group. The precise location of this breeding population remains unknown. The birds ultimately derived from Scarlet Macaw populations far south of Chaco and reached the region through long-distance exchange networks.
Collections & Reconstruction: Pueblo Bonito has produced approximately 35 macaws plus 2 thick-billed parrots in recent reassessments of the collections. The reconstructed upper story is interpretive.

features.name: Room 28
features.title: Room 28 — Cylinder Jar Cache & Cacao Residue
features.phase: Old Bonito Construction • Late 11th–Early 12th Century Cache Deposit
features.masonry: Multi-Phase Old Bonito & Remodeled Masonry (Wall Rebuilding, Subdivision & Reconstructed Upper Story)
features.dendroDates: Old Bonito construction; late 11th–early 12th century cache deposit
features.artifacts: Excavations recovered approximately 174 whole ceramic vessels from Room 28, including ~111–112 Chacoan cylinder jars (with roughly 99 concentrated together on a raised storage shelf/area), alongside ceramic bowls and pitchers, burned during a termination event around AD 1100. Chemical residue analysis tested five cylinder jar sherds from Pueblo Bonito and detected theobromine (Theobroma cacao) in three of them.
features.summary: The surviving Room 28 measures just under 8 m long and approximately 2.75 m wide at the surface. Earlier construction phases indicate that Room 28 and adjoining space were originally part of a substantially longer Old Bonito room before later partitioning and remodeling. Room 28 underwent several construction phases, including wall rebuilding, subdivision, and the addition of an upper story (reconstructed) during the 11th century. Excavators recovered approximately 174 whole ceramic vessels from Room 28, including 112 Chacoan cylinder jars. Around AD 1100, many of the vessels were deliberately arranged and burned during a termination event; roughly 99 cylinder jars were concentrated on a shelf or raised storage area, accompanied by turquoise and shell materials. Chemical analysis tested five pottery sherds from Pueblo Bonito; three produced theobromine, demonstrating the preparation or consumption of cacao beverages at Chaco, which reached the region through long-distance exchange networks originating in Mesoamerica.
features.excavator: George H. Pepper (Hyde Exploring Expedition, 1896; Pepper 1920) • Residue analysis: Patricia L. Crown & W. Jeffrey Hurst (2009, PNAS)
features.footprint_label: Surviving surface room: just under 8 m long × approx. 2.75 m wide (originally part of a longer Old Bonito room before later partitioning)
features.tinyEra: OLD BONITO CONSTRUCTION • LATE 11TH–EARLY 12TH CENTURY CACHE DEPOSIT
features.tinyTitle: ROOM 28 — CYLINDER JAR CACHE & CACAO RESIDUE
features.description: Originally part of the early Old Bonito northern arc and later remodeled and subdivided, with an added upper story. Excavators recovered approximately 174 whole ceramic vessels from Room 28, including ~111–112 Chacoan cylinder jars (with roughly 99 concentrated on a shelf or raised storage area) alongside bowls and pitchers, deliberately arranged and burned during a termination event around AD 1100. Chemical analysis tested five pottery sherds from Pueblo Bonito and detected theobromine—the biomarker for Theobroma cacao—in three of them.
keyPoints: Architecture: Earlier construction phases indicate that Room 28 and adjoining space were originally part of a substantially longer Old Bonito room before later partitioning and remodeling. Room 28 underwent several construction phases, including wall rebuilding, subdivision, and the addition of an upper story (interpretive reconstruction) during the 11th century.

Cylinder Jar Cache: Excavators recovered approximately 174 whole ceramic vessels from Room 28, including 112 Chacoan cylinder jars. Around AD 1100, many of the vessels were deliberately arranged and burned during a termination event. Roughly 99 cylinder jars were concentrated on a shelf or raised storage area, accompanied by turquoise and shell materials.

Cacao Evidence: Chemical analysis tested five pottery sherds from Pueblo Bonito. Three produced theobromine, demonstrating the preparation or consumption of cacao beverages at Chaco. Cacao could not have been grown locally and must have reached Chaco through long-distance exchange networks originating in Mesoamerica.

features.name: Room 53
features.title: Room 53 — Northern Burial Cluster Chamber
features.phase: Stage I: Old Bonito Crescent (AD 850–950)
features.dendroDates: Mid-9th to 10th century (approx. AD 850–950, Old Bonito core, est.)
features.artifacts: Multiple elite human burials, Red Mesa & Gallup Black-on-white bowls, turquoise-and-jet mosaic inlays, shell bracelets, and bone awls.
features.summary: Situated immediately north of Rooms 32 and 33 in the Old Bonito core, Room 53 forms part of the Western Burial Cluster. Bioarchaeological analysis (Plog & Heitman 2010) shows individuals buried in this cluster had distinct dietary isotopes and extraordinary mortuary wealth.
features.excavator: George H. Pepper (Hyde Exploring Expedition, 1897) • NPS / HABS Survey

features.name: Room 33
features.title: Room 33 — Matrilineal Mortuary Crypt
features.phase: Stage I: Old Bonito Nucleus (AD 850–935 • Burials AD 800–1130)
features.masonry: Type I Unshaped Tabular Sandstone Slabs in Thick Mud Mortar
features.dendroDates: Construction: Stage I (c. AD 850–935; adjacent Room 32 ceiling poles AD 862–919) • AMS ¹⁴C on burials: AD 800–1130 (Kennett et al. 2017)
features.artifacts: 14 human burials: Burial 14 (>11,200 turquoise & >3,300 shell beads/pendants, abalone shells, Strombus shell trumpet) and Burial 13 (>5,800 turquoise pieces) below wood plank floor, plus 12 interments above floor (>56,000 total turquoise items in Room 33, carved wooden flutes, turquoise-mosaic cylinder basket, ceremonial staffs).
features.summary: Excavated by George H. Pepper in 1896 (Pepper 1909, 1920), Room 33 has a georeferenced polygon footprint of 1.9 × 2.0 m (3.8 m²; Pepper 1909 recorded interior wall lengths of N 6 ft 3 in, S 5 ft 10 in, E 6 ft 10 in, W 6 ft 0 in, with a 5 ft 6 in [1.68 m] ground-floor ceiling beneath Upper Room 58). Beneath a hand-hewn pine plank floor lay two adult males in clean yellow sand: Burial 14 (AMS ¹⁴C dated AD 800–850, accompanied by >11,200 turquoise and >3,300 marine shell ornaments) and Burial 13 (>5,800 turquoise pieces). Above the plank floor lay 12 subsequent interments (14 individuals total in Room 33, with >56,000 turquoise items). Ancient DNA sequencing (Kennett et al. 2017, Nature Communications 8:14115) reconstructed complete mitochondrial genomes from 9 individuals—all 9 sharing the identical rare mtDNA haplotype B2y1—and nuclear SNP data from 6 individuals confirming first- and second-degree lineal kin (mother–daughter and grandmother–grandson) buried across ~330 years (AD 800–1130).
features.excavator: George H. Pepper (Hyde Exploring Expedition, 1896; Pepper 1909, 1920) • Archaeogenomics: Kennett et al. (2017, Nature Communications)
features.footprint_label: 1.9 × 2.0 m (3.8 m² polygon; Pepper 1909 interior walls: N 6 ft 3 in, S 5 ft 10 in, E 6 ft 10 in, W 6 ft 0 in [~1.8 × 2.0 m]; 5 ft 6 in [1.68 m] ground ceiling)
features.description: Ground-story Old Bonito mortuary chamber beneath reconstructed Upper Room 58, excavated by George H. Pepper in 1896. Contained 14 human burials spanning AD 800–1130 and more than 56,000 turquoise items; complete mtDNA genomes from 9 sequenced individuals were 100% identical (haplotype B2y1; Kennett et al. 2017).

features.name: Room 326
features.title: Room 326 — Western Burial Cluster Chamber
features.phase: Old Bonito Architectural Block • Approx. AD 860–935 Construction (Modified in Later Occupation)
features.masonry: Early Pueblo Bonito Masonry with Later Alterations
features.dendroDates: Approx. AD 860–935 architectural construction; later modifications & mortuary use
features.artifacts: Later reassessment of the human remains associated with Room 326 identified 12 individuals: 11 adults (10 females and 1 male) and 1 infant. Older excavation inventories reported 11 individuals. Formed part of the larger western burial cluster that also included Rooms 320, 329, and 330.
features.summary: Georeferenced room footprint approx. 4.0 × 9.1 m (36.4 m²). The room belongs to one of Pueblo Bonito’s earliest western architectural blocks (approx. AD 860–935 construction) and was modified during later occupation, including sealed openings and changes connecting Room 326 with neighboring rooms. Later reassessment of the human remains associated with Room 326 identified 12 individuals: 11 adults and one infant (the adults include 10 females and one male). Older excavation inventories reported 11 individuals, which accounts for differences in published burial counts. Room 326 formed part of the larger western burial cluster that also included Rooms 320, 329, and 330.
features.excavator: Neil M. Judd (National Geographic Society, 1924) • Smithsonian / NPS Survey
features.description: Belongs to one of Pueblo Bonito’s earliest western architectural blocks (approx. Room 326 formed part of the larger western burial cluster that also included Rooms 320, 329, and 330.

Early Pueblo Bonito masonry with later alterations, including sealed openings and changes connecting Room 326 with neighboring rooms (reconstructed 2-story wall height).
Mortuary Use: Later reassessment of the human remains associated with Room 326 identified 12 individuals: 11 adults and one infant. The adults include 10 females and one male.

Excavation Inventories & Cluster: Older excavation inventories reported 11 individuals, which accounts for differences in published burial counts. Room 326 formed part of the larger western burial cluster that also included Rooms 320, 329, and 330.

features.name: Threatening Rock (Tsé Bíyah Aniiʼáhí)
features.title: Threatening Rock (Tsé Bíyah Aniiʼáhí) — 1941 Cliff Collapse & Prehistoric Retaining Terrace
features.phase: Geological / Stabilized by Chacoan Engineers c. AD 1050; Collapsed Jan 22, 1941
features.masonry: Late Cretaceous Cliff House Sandstone Monolith & Chacoan Masonry Retaining Terrace
features.dendroDates: 11th-century bracing terrace (c. AD 1040–1085) • Collapsed January 22, 1941 at 3:10 PM
features.artifacts: ~30,000-ton detached Cliff House Sandstone monolith (~45 m long × ~11 m thick × ~30 m high) and prehistoric earth-and-masonry retaining terrace with vertical ponderosa pine posts at its base.
features.summary: Known in Navajo as Tsé Bíyah Aniiʼáhí ('Rock Braced Underneath'), this ~30,000-ton detached slab of Late Cretaceous Cliff House Sandstone measured ~30 m (100 ft) high, ~45 m (148 ft) long, and ~11 m (36 ft) thick (~495 m² basal slab plan) directly behind Pueblo Bonito's northeast wall. Chacoan builders constructed a masonry-and-timber retaining terrace along its base. On January 22, 1941, following winter frost-wedging and precipitation, Threatening Rock collapsed across a 45.0 × 24.0 m (950.0 m²) talus zone, destroying ~30 m of the outer northern wall and crushing ~65 northeastern rooms.
features.excavator: Neil M. Judd & NPS Engineering / Geological Survey (1924–1941; Schumm & Chorley 1964)
features.footprint_label: 45.0 × 24.0 m talus collapse polygon (950.0 m²); detached sandstone monolith ~45 m long × ~11 m thick × ~30 m (100 ft) high (~30,000 tons)
features.tinyEra: 11TH-CENTURY RETAINING TERRACE • COLLAPSED JAN 22, 1941

features.name: South Refuse Mounds & Water-Control Channels
features.title: East & West South Mounds — Stratified Masonry-Walled Platforms & Water-Control Channels
features.phase: Stage III–IV (AD 1050–1115)
features.masonry: Formal Masonry Retaining Walls Enclosing Stratified Ash, Potsherds, Construction Debris & Water Channels
features.dendroDates: Classic to Late Bonito phase (c. AD 1050–1115; Wills et al. 2016, Crown 2016)
features.artifacts: Stratified Chaco Black-on-white and corrugated ceramic sherds, turquoise lapidary debitage, faunal bone, masonry retaining walls, and lateral water-diversion channels.
features.summary: Immediately south of Pueblo Bonito's front wall stand two rectangular masonry-walled mounds (combined bounding footprint 88.0 × 26.0 m, 1,850.0 m²) separated by a central gap. Excavations by Neil M. Judd (1922) and the University of New Mexico (Wills et al. 2016; Crown 2016) documented formal exterior masonry walls, internal stratigraphy of ash, ceramics, and construction debris, and adjacent water-control trenches.
features.excavator: Neil M. Judd (1922; Judd 1954, 1964) & UNM Chaco Stratigraphy Project (W.H. Wills & Patricia L. Crown, 2006–2016)
features.tinyEra: CLASSIC TO LATE BONITO PHASE • APPROX. AD 1050–1115
